# Lobular carcinoma in situ

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Breast disorders > Lobular carcinoma in situ*

[Original Article Link](/library/6G0jZ3)

---

## Summary

Lobular <u>carcinoma in situ</u> (LCIS) is a noninvasive proliferative lesion of the <u>breast</u> that arises from the <u>terminal ductal lobular units</u>. It is typically asymptomatic; detected incidentally on <u>core needle biopsy</u>, most commonly in <u>premenopausal</u> women aged ∼ 50 years. Histologically, LCIS is divided into <u>classic LCIS</u> and <u>LCIS variants</u>, which include <u>pleomorphic LCIS</u> and <u>florid LCIS</u>. Although LCIS is a nonmalignant lesion, it is a <u>risk factor</u> for invasive <u>breast cancer</u> in the <u>ipsilateral</u> and <u>contralateral</u> <u>breasts</u>. Management is challenging, as the data on risk <u>stratification</u> of LCIS and the long-term benefits of treatment options are lacking. Treatment options include close clinical surveillance, surgical excision to rule out concurrent <u>breast cancer</u>, and prophylactic strategies such as <u>chemotherapy</u> or <u>bilateral mastectomy</u> to minimize the risk of developing <u>breast cancer</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* Median age at diagnosis: 50 years [[2]](/library/tqcXZd0)[[3]](/library/lP1vUS0)[[4]](/library/twbXkD)

* Approx. 85% of cases occur in <u>premenopausal</u> women.

* LCIS is a <u>risk factor</u> for invasive <u>breast cancer</u>. 

* The annual <u>incidence</u> of <u>breast cancer</u> in patients with LCIS is ∼ 2% per year.  [[2]](/library/tqcXZd0)[[5]](/library/h81cmi0)[[6]](/library/NP1-US0)

* Invasive <u>breast cancer</u> can occur in the <u>ipsilateral</u> or <u>contralateral</u> <u>breast</u> in patients with LCIS.

* LCIS has a lower risk of subsequent <u>invasive carcinoma</u> compared to <u>DCIS</u>.





> [!TIP]
> LCIS was previously classified as a premalignant lesion (i.e., <u>Tis</u>). It is now considered a benign entity and has been removed from the 8<sup>th</sup> edition of the AJCC <u>TNM</u> <u>cancer staging</u> system. [[7]](/library/p9bLoD)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

## Classification

| <br>Histological classification of LCIS [[8]](/library/sqct-W0)[[9]](/library/p30Ljf)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Types |  | Characteristics |
| <br>Classic LCIS (CLCIS) |  | <br><br>* Small, uniform, discohesive cells with round or oval <u>nuclei</u><br><br>* Cytologic dyshesion, intracytoplasmic <u>vacuoles</u><br><br>* <u>Estrogen</u>/<u>progesterone</u> <u>receptor</u>-positive<br><br>* Decreased <u>E-cadherin</u> expression<br><br>* Distention of the <u>terminal duct</u> lobular units<br><br><br> |
| <br>LCIS variants [[8]](/library/sqct-W0)<br> | <br>Pleomorphic LCIS (PLCIS) | <br><br>* Larger cells with <u>nuclear pleomorphism</u><br><br>* Cytologic dyshesion, intracytoplasmic <u>vacuoles</u><br><br>* Apocrine features may be present.<br><br>* Central <u>necrosis</u> and calcifications<br><br><br> |
| <br>Florid LCIS (FLCIS) | <br><br>* Marked distortion and distention of the <u>terminal duct</u> lobular units<br><br>* Form a mass-like appearance<br><br>* Apocrine features may be present.<br><br>* Central <u>necrosis</u> and microcalcifications<br><br><br> |  |

---

## Clinical features

* Asymptomatic; no specific findings (no mass or calcifications)

* Approx. 55% are multicentric and approx. 35% are bilateral [[3]](/library/lP1vUS0)[[9]](/library/p30Ljf)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Classic LCIS</u> is typically not apparent on <u>clinical breast examination</u> or imaging. In PLCIS, <u>pleomorphic</u> calcifications may be seen on <u>mammography</u>. [[3]](/library/lP1vUS0)

---

## Diagnosis

* LCIS is usually detected incidentally during <u>biopsy</u> for another abnormality.  [[3]](/library/lP1vUS0)[[10]](/library/Qe1uAf0)[[11]](/library/S81yNi0)

* <u>Immunohistochemistry</u> ;  [[3]](/library/lP1vUS0)[[5]](/library/h81cmi0)[[11]](/library/S81yNi0)

* <u>E-cadherin</u>: negative

* p120 <u>catenin</u>: diffuse <u>cytoplasmic</u> staining

* <u>Receptor</u> testing: may show <u>estrogen</u> and <u>progesterone</u> positive, <u>ERBB2</u> negative  [[3]](/library/lP1vUS0)

## Treatment

Quality evidence on risk <u>stratification</u> and optimal management of LCIS is lacking. Refer patients with LCIS to oncology. Shared-decision making is recommended when selecting a treatment strategy.




### Close clinical surveillance [[3]](/library/lP1vUS0)[[5]](/library/h81cmi0)




* <u>Clinical breast examination</u> every 6–12 months

* Women ≥ 30 years [[5]](/library/h81cmi0)

* Annual <u>mammogram</u> with or without <u>digital breast tomosynthesis</u>

* Alternatively, <u>breast</u> <u>MRI</u> may be considered in patients with additional <u>risk factors for breast cancer</u> (e.g., <u>family history</u> of <u>breast cancer</u>).





### Surgical excision (<u>breast conservation surgery</u>) [[11]](/library/S81yNi0)[[12]](/library/J81sni0)




* Consider for <u>LCIS variants</u> (to rule out concurrent invasive <u>breast cancer</u>).

* The need to achieve <u>R0</u> resection is unclear as the recurrence rates for close or positive margins are not significant.





> [!TIP]
> Surgical excision to rule out associated invasive <u>breast cancer</u> is not routinely recommended for <u>classic LCIS</u>. [[12]](/library/J81sni0)




### <u>Breast cancer</u> risk-reduction options [[2]](/library/tqcXZd0)[[6]](/library/NP1-US0)




#### <u>Chemoprevention</u>




* Consider for patients < 65 years of age who opt for a risk-reducing strategy. [[6]](/library/NP1-US0)

* Agents  [[10]](/library/Qe1uAf0)[[13]](/library/q81Cni0)

* <u>Selective estrogen receptor modulator</u> (e.g., <u>tamoxifen</u>, <u>raloxifene</u>)

* <u>Aromatase inhibitor</u> (e.g., <u>exemestane</u>)





#### Bilateral <u>prophylactic mastectomy</u>



* Consider in patients with additional <u>risk factors for breast cancer</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Although <u>chemoprevention</u> and bilateral <u>prophylactic mastectomy</u> significantly decrease the risk of <u>breast cancer</u> in patients with LCIS, they are associated with significant adverse effects and the impact of these interventions on overall survival is modest. [[2]](/library/tqcXZd0)[[6]](/library/NP1-US0)
